content: Data on the total number of health workers should be used as a denominator, regardless of whether information on active health workers is available. In cases where data on foreign-trained health workers is unavailable, the number of foreign-born health workers beginning practice can serve as a substitute. For the total number of active health workers, data from the middle or end of the year should be utilized. Glossary: Foreign-born health worker: A health worker born outside the country of practice. Foreign-trained health worker: A health worker trained outside the country of practice. Newly active health worker: A health worker who has recently entered the workforce. Occupation: The specific role or job of a health worker. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Ministry of Health databases Health workforce registries or databases Professional council, chamber, or association registers Aggregate data from health facilities (e.g., routine administrative records, Health Management Information Systems, District Health Information Systems, censuses, and surveys) Further Information and References: OECD et al. (2016), WHO et al. (2009), WHO (2015c) Additional references: USAID and Capacity Plus (2015), EU Joint Action on Health Workforce Planning and Forecasting (2016a), OECD (2015a, 2016) The voluntary exit rate from the health labor market is defined as the ratio of active health workers who voluntarily leave the health sector to the total stock of active health workers. This includes those who leave due to emigration, temporary leave, sector changes, early retirement, or other voluntary reasons. Early retirement is considered voluntary, while retirement at the standard age is classified as involuntary. Numerator: Number of health workers who became inactive in the health sector due to voluntary reasons. Denominator: Total number of active health workers (headcount). Disaggregation: By occupation and sex. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Health workforce registries or databases Professional council registers Aggregate data from health facilities (e.g., administrative records, Health Management Information Systems, District Health Information Systems, censuses, and surveys) Pension or retirement administration units Mortality records Further Information and References: WHO et al. (2009), WHO (2007), EU Joint Action on Health Workforce Planning and Forecasting (2015) Additional references: Early retirement is excluded from this indicator and counted under voluntary exits. Numerator: Number of health workers who became inactive due to involuntary reasons. Denominator: Total number of active health workers (headcount). Disaggregation: By occupation and sex. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Health workforce registries or databases Professional council registers Aggregate data from health facilities Pension or retirement administration units Mortality records Further Information and References: WHO et al. (2009), WHO (2007), EU Joint Action on Health Workforce Planning and Forecasting (2015) Additional references: WHO (2015a, 2015c), USAID and Capacity Plus (2015), WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific (2007) The unemployment rate for health workers is defined as the proportion of trained health workers who are unemployed but actively seeking employment and available to work. This includes new graduates not yet employed. For unemployed individuals, the occupation refers to their last job or the field in which they are seeking work. Numerator: Number of trained health workers currently unemployed. Denominator: Total number of active and unemployed health workers. Disaggregation: By occupation, sex, and subnational level. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Employment office statistics Labor force surveys National health accounts surveys Population census data Further Information and References: International Labour Organization (2013), Eurostat (2017a), WHO et al. (2009) Additional references: Unfilled positions must have been vacant for at least six months, with active recruitment efforts underway. Numerator: Number of unfilled funded full-time posts. Denominator: Total number of funded full-time posts (filled and unfilled). Disaggregation: By occupation and subnational level. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Labor force surveys Health facility assessments Employment offices or job agencies Further Information and References: WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific (2007), WHO et al. (2009), Eurostat (2010) The standard working hours indicator reports the number of standard working hours per week as defined by national laws or standards. Disaggregation by occupation is recommended if regulations vary by job type. Data Reporting Frequency: Every three years Potential Data Sources: Employment laws, policies, and regulations Collective agreements Further Information and References: Lee et al. Numerator: Number of active health workers with part-time contracts. Denominator: Total number of active health workers. Disaggregation: By occupation and facility ownership. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Facility databases or surveys Health workforce registries Labor force surveys Public service human resource and payroll administrations Further Information and References: OECD (2017g) The existence of regulations on working hours and conditions assesses whether national or subnational policies regulate aspects such as maximum working days, overtime pay, and annual leave entitlements. Data Reporting Frequency: Every three years Potential Data Sources: Employment laws, policies, and regulations Further Information and References: The World Bank (2017a) The existence of regulations on minimum wage evaluates whether health workers are eligible for a minimum wage under national or subnational laws. Data Reporting Frequency: Every three years Potential Data Sources: Employment laws, policies, and regulations Further Information and References: International Labour Organization (2008) The existence of regulations on social protection examines whether policies address maternity leave, parental leave, childcare support, and other social protections for health workers. Data Reporting Frequency: Every three years Potential Data Sources: Employment laws, policies, and regulations Social security records Further Information and References: OECD (2017e) The existence of regulations on dual practice assesses whether policies govern health workers engaging in private practice alongside public employment. Data Reporting Frequency: Every three years Potential Data Sources: Employment laws, policies, and regulations Further Information and References: McPake et al. (2016) The existence of regulations on compulsory service evaluates whether policies mandate health workers to serve in specific programs or areas, with or without incentives. Data Reporting Frequency: Every three years Potential Data Sources: Employment laws, policies, and regulations Further Information and References: Frehywot et al. Data Reporting Frequency: Every three years Potential Data Sources: Government or legislative records Further Information and References: International Labour Office et al. (2002) The number of attacks on the health-care system tracks incidents of physical or psychological violence against health facilities, providers, transport, or patients. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Workplace violence surveys Police records Further Information and References: WHO (2017a), International Labour Office et al. Data Reporting Frequency: Annual Potential Data Sources: Ministry of Health and Finance records National Statistics Office records Further Information and References: OECD et al. (2011, 2016), WHO (2007)
